claims.text: The initial composite contains 20 vol% W and 80 vol% Cu.
Liquid-metal infiltration produces an as-sintered W–Cu composite with approximately 100 µm grains.
The intervention adds 0.5 vol% graphene nanoplatelets at W–Cu interfaces by slurry infiltration before Cu infiltration.
Adding 0.5 vol% interfacial graphene nanoplatelets will increase overall thermal conductivity by at least 10%.
The graphene-modified composite will retain mechanical durability.
The graphene-modified composite will retain irradiation resistance.
The hypothesis should hold from 300 to 700 K in atmospheric or vacuum fusion-joint environments.
The hypothesis should hold under neutron irradiation up to 5 dpa at 573 K.
The graphene nanoplatelets will form a continuous percolating network that bridges W grains and the Cu matrix across their interfaces.
Graphene has high in-plane thermal conductivity.
Interfacial graphene will reduce W–Cu interface thermal resistance.
A percolating graphene network will create continuous heat-conduction paths through the composite.
Strong C–C bonds and good graphene dispersion will preserve the composite's mechanical strength.
Strong C–C bonds and good graphene dispersion will resist radiation-induced damage.
At 600 K, thermal conductivity will increase from approximately 300 W/m·K to at least 330 W/m·K.
Tensile strength and Vickers hardness will each vary by less than 5% relative to the graphene-free baseline.
Post-irradiation embrittlement will remain within 10% of the baseline.
The effect should hold for graphene loadings of 0.2–1 vol% and nanoplatelets approximately 5 µm wide and 5 nm thick.
The expected effect size is extrapolated from Cu–graphene studies.
The magnitude of the effect depends on the quality of graphene dispersion at W–Cu interfaces.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis predicts a gain of at least 10%, but the stated rule only falsifies gains below 5%, leaving gains from 5% to under 10% inconsistent with the prediction but not classified as falsifying.
Irradiation resistance is claimed through 5 dpa, whereas the proposed experiment tests only 1 dpa; the experiment therefore cannot decisively assess the upper claimed irradiation boundary.
